title: Yitro: the last word is inside (Exodus 20:14)
hookLine: the final commandment, not to covet, governs the heart rather than the hands
tomorrow: Mishpatim: straight after Sinai, the details

cards: Scroll through anyone's feed for five minutes: the kitchen renovation, the beach in Greece, the promotion, the couple who never seem to argue. Nobody stole anything. Nobody lied.

And still a phone gets put down by someone feeling a little smaller, wanting what's theirs. Most of the Ten Words are about things you could see someone do or not do: make an idol, work on Shabbat, steal, lie in court.
The tenth is different. Nobody can see you break it.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation, the tenth begins: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house"; then the list: his wife, his servants, his ox, his donkey, anything that belongs to your neighbor. In Hebrew, lo tachmod.
The first word was anochi, I, God's own self.
The last word reaches into your own self. Abraham ibn Ezra, the medieval Spanish commentator, asked the honest question: how can anyone be commanded not to feel something? Wanting just happens.

teach.h: IBN EZRA: THE VILLAGER AND PRINCESS.
teach.b: A villager sees a beautiful princess pass by. He doesn't lie awake longing to marry her, because he knows it's simply not his world.
In the same way, says Ibn Ezra, a person who truly understands that what's yours is yours by God's gift will stop reaching for what isn't. The wanting quiets down because the frame has changed.

The early rabbis and Maimonides read the verse more narrowly in law: you break it when you act on the wanting, pressuring someone until they hand over what's theirs. Deuteronomy adds a second verb, about desire itself.

teach.h: FROM THE HANDS TO THE HEART.
teach.b: So there's a range of readings, from the hands to the heart. Either way, the list that starts at Sinai ends inside the chest.
And with that, Yitro is done: an outsider's wisdom, one heart, eagles' wings, the first word, and the last.

how: Jewish law, following the Mekhilta and Maimonides, holds that the command not to covet is broken by acting on the desire, such as pressuring an owner to sell; Jewish ethical writers also treat envy itself as a trait to work on.

s: the tenth commandment is about something no one else can see
most of the others are visible acts; the tenth reaches into the heart.
Ibn Ezra said no one can control wanting, so the command is impossible
his parable says wanting quiets when you know a thing isn't yours.
all Jewish readings agree the tenth is only about feelings

games.q: a villager sees a princess ride by. you're Ibn Ezra. why doesn't he lie awake longing to marry her?
o: he's too busy with his fields.
he knows she's simply not his world.
games.why: it's not on the table, so the wanting doesn't take hold. Ibn Ezra says knowing what's yours by God's gift does the same.

practice: Name, without scolding yourself, one thing in someone else's life you've quietly been wanting: their house, their job, their marriage, their calm.

Then turn to what's actually in your hands right now, a person, a skill, a small comfort, this breath, and hold that instead. If you pray, you can give thanks for one of those things, and let the envy loosen a little.

wordCard.voice: Yitro. The portion we finish today, whose Ten Words begin with God's I and end inside the human heart.

orig.note: Hebrew: thou shalt not covet, the tenth of the Ten Words.
